etymology: A 2010s variation of the old wake-up call rise and shine (itself early twentieth-century, often military). Rise and grind spread through fitness and entrepreneurial social media as a morning mantra of hustle culture: get up early, work harder than everyone else, never stop. It appeared on gym walls, coffee mugs, and countless Instagram captions at 5 a.m.; the investor Daymond John used it as the title of a 2018 book. Gen Z later mocked it alongside "hustle porn."
biblical_def: Rise and grind is the hustle-culture alarm clock: up before dawn, straight to work or the gym, outwork everyone, rest when you are dead. It is posted as a badge of discipline and ambition. The Christian observation: half of this is wisdom and half is idolatry, and the halves need separating. Scripture loves early rising and hard work. The sluggard is mocked for loving his bed: "How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?" (Pro 6:9). The virtuous woman "riseth also while it is yet night" (Pro 31:15). The Lord Jesus Himself, "rising up a great while before day," went out to pray (Mar 1:35). Note what He did with the early hour: He prayed before He worked. But Scripture also contains a sentence that reads like a rebuke written for this slogan: "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep" (Psa 127:2). The grind that never stops, that measures a man’s worth by hours and output, that treats sleep and Sabbath as weakness, is labour without the Lord, and "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it" (Psa 127:1). A father teaches his son to get up early, to work hard, and to begin the day with God; and to know that he is not what he produces, that rest is commanded, and that the Lord gives to His beloved even in their sleep.
webster_summary: Millennial hustle-culture mantra (2010s; from rise and shine) for early rising and relentless work; diligence and early prayer are biblical (Pro 6:9; Mar 1:35), but labour without the Lord and without rest is vain (Psa 127:1-2).
webster_full: RISE AND GRIND, phr. (Millennial hustle-culture slang, 2010s) A morning motto urging early rising and relentless work or training. Related: hustle culture, grindset, "team no sleep."

Webster (1828), root grind: GRIND, verb transitive preterit tense and participle passive ground. [This word, if n is radical, may be allied to rend; if not, it coincides with grate; to make smooth, as mollis in Latin , allied to molo.] 1. To break and reduce to fine particles or powder by friction; to comminute by attrition; to triturate. Take the millstones and grind meal. Isaiah 47:2 . We say, to grind meal, but this is an elliptical phrase. The true phrase is, to grind corn to meal. 2. To break and reduce to small pieces by the teeth. 3. […]
Decode for parents: teach the early hour and the hard day, and teach that worth is not output and rest is commanded.
scriptures: Pro 6:9
How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?
She riseth also while it is yet night, and giveth meat to her household, and a portion to her maidens.
Mar 1:35
And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.
Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
corruption_summary: Rise and grind joins true diligence to the idolatry of endless work; Scripture praises the early riser who prays first and calls the sleepless grind without the Lord vain.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is work as identity and salvation. The grind mindset promises that enough effort will produce worth, wealth, and meaning, and it treats rest as failure. That is the treadmill of Babel, building a name by labour. Scripture’s word for it is vanity: rising early and sitting up late without the Lord produces bread of sorrows. The grind also tends to crowd out prayer, family, and the Lord’s Day, the very things that make work meaningful.

The recovery is diligence under grace. Christians should be the hardest workers in any room, not to earn their worth but because they already have it. Begin the day with God, as Jesus did; work heartily as to the Lord; stop at evening; keep the Sabbath; and sleep well, trusting Him. Teach the young that discipline is a fruit of the Spirit, not a brand, and that the Lord who neither slumbers nor sleeps lets His people do both.
roots_summary: Old English grindan (to crush) → grind (hard, monotonous work) → "rise and shine" → 2010s hustle-culture rise and grind.
roots_lines: Old English grindan — to rub, to crush small
19th c.: the grind — hard, monotonous work or study
Early 20th c.: "rise and shine"; 2010s: rise and grind on gym walls and Instagram
2018: Daymond John, Rise and Grind; later Gen Z "hustle porn" mockery
Biblical anchor: rising up a great while before day … and there prayed (Mar 1:35); so he giveth his beloved sleep (Psa 127:2)
usage: "5 a.m. workout. Rise and grind."
Jesus rose early, and prayed first (Mar 1:35).
It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows (Psa 127:2).

etymology: Clipped from bourgeois (French, a town-dweller; in Marxist use, the property-owning middle class). In African-American usage from at least the 1960s–70s, bougie (also boujee, bourgie) described someone with upper-class pretensions, putting on airs. Millennials broadened it in the 2010s to anything pretentiously upscale or fancy ("bougie brunch," "bougie candles"), sometimes as self-mockery; the 2016 hit "Bad and Boujee" spread the spelling boujee.
biblical_def: Bougie means fancy in a way that wants to be noticed: the expensive candle, the artisanal brunch, the person who acts above his station. It can be a mild insult or a cheerful confession ("I’m being bougie and getting the good cheese"). The Christian observation: enjoying good things is not a sin, and pretension is. Scripture permits enjoyment of God’s gifts; He "giveth us richly all things to enjoy" (1Ti 6:17). The good cheese is a mercy. But the word’s root idea is putting on airs, presenting oneself as richer or more refined than one is or than others, and Scripture is pointed about it. "There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches" (Pro 13:7). James rebukes the church that seats the man "with a gold ring, in goodly apparel" in the best place and tells the poor man to stand, "are ye not then partial in yourselves" (Jas 2:4). Paul tells believers, "Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate" (Rom 12:16). The bougie temptation for Millennials was often lifestyle display, curated taste, financed on credit, photographed to signal status. A father teaches his children: enjoy good things with thanks, buy what you can afford, never despise people with less, and never pretend to be more than you are. The truly refined person is the one who makes everyone at the table feel welcome.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (AAVE bougie from bourgeois; 2010s broadening) for pretentiously upscale; enjoying good gifts is allowed (1Ti 6:17), but putting on airs and partiality are not (Pro 13:7; Jas 2:4).
webster_full: BOUGIE, adj. (AAVE from 1960s–70s; Millennial broadening, 2010s; also boujee, bourgie; clipped from bourgeois) Pretentiously upscale; aspiring to or displaying upper-class taste. "That’s a bougie brunch spot."
No Webster 1828 entry located for the root bourgeois (a French borrowing).
Decode for parents: enjoy good things gratefully; watch for display, debt, and contempt for those with less.
scriptures: Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;
Pro 13:7
There is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself poor, yet hath great riches.
Jas 2:4
Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?
Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits.
Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud.
corruption_summary: Bougie names pretension and status display; Scripture allows grateful enjoyment of good gifts and condemns putting on airs and partiality toward the rich.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is status by consumption. Bougie living, especially when performed online and financed by debt, makes taste a ladder and invites contempt for those lower on it. It is the old sin of pride in a new wardrobe, and the old folly of appearing rich while having nothing. James’s church fell into the same trap when it honoured the gold ring and shamed the poor man.

The recovery is gratitude without pretension. "Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud" (Pro 16:19). Christians may enjoy good food and beautiful things as gifts, and they should be generous and humble with them: share the good cheese, set an extra place, sit with the lowly. Teach the young that refinement is a matter of manners and kindness, not price tags.
roots_summary: Old French borgeis (town-dweller) → bourgeois → Marxist bourgeoisie → AAVE bougie (pretentious) → 2010s Millennial broadening; boujee (2016).
roots_lines: Late Latin burgus (fortified town) → Old French borgeis — a citizen of a town
19th c.: Marxist bourgeoisie — the property-owning middle class
1960s–70s: AAVE bougie — putting on upper-class airs
2010s: Millennial bougie for anything fancy; 2016: "Bad and Boujee"
Biblical anchor: there is that maketh himself rich, yet hath nothing (Pro 13:7); mind not high things (Rom 12:16)
usage: "A forty-dollar candle? So bougie."
God giveth us richly all things to enjoy (1Ti 6:17); enjoy without airs.
Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate (Rom 12:16).

etymology: From the 1995 comedy Friday (directed by F. Gary Gray, co-written by Ice Cube), in which Ice Cube’s character dismisses a neighbourhood moocher named Felicia with "Bye, Felicia." The line circulated in Black culture through the 2000s and exploded as a meme around 2014 on social media and reality television; the 2015 film Straight Outta Compton included a nod to it. It means a dismissive goodbye to someone the speaker considers unimportant or annoying.
biblical_def: "Bye, Felicia" is a dismissal: a breezy, cutting goodbye to someone you consider beneath your attention, whose name you do not care to know. In the film the joke was that Felicia was always asking for something; in the meme, any annoying or rejected person becomes Felicia. The Christian observation: the phrase is funny because it is contemptuous, and contempt is precisely what the Lord Jesus warned against. "Whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council" (Mat 5:22): Raca, "empty head," was the dismissive word of His day. Scripture’s view of the person the world dismisses is the opposite of the meme’s. The Lord stopped for the blind beggar the crowd told to be quiet (Mar 10:48-49). He knew the names of His sheep: "he calleth his own sheep by name" (Joh 10:3). Paul commands, "in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves" (Php 2:3). There is a right way to end a conversation, to refuse a request, or even to leave a relationship, and Scripture has room for firm boundaries; Jesus Himself sometimes went away from those who rejected Him. But the posture of "Bye, Felicia" is not firmness; it is a sneer. A father teaches his children to say no clearly, to leave toxic situations, and never to treat anyone as a nameless nuisance, because every Felicia has a name and a soul, and Christ died for people the world dismisses.
webster_summary: Millennial meme (from Friday, 1995; viral c. 2014) for a contemptuous dismissal of someone deemed unimportant; Scripture condemns the Raca of contempt (Mat 5:22) and esteems others better than ourselves (Php 2:3). Reject.
webster_full: BYE, FELICIA, phr. (Millennial slang, from the film Friday, 1995; viral c. 2014) A dismissive farewell to someone regarded as unimportant, annoying, or unwelcome.
No Webster 1828 entry located for the root good-by / bye in the sense of farewell (the 1828 bye is an unrelated word meaning a dwelling).
Decode for parents: firm boundaries are fine; contempt for a person is not.
scriptures: Mat 5:22

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.

And many charged him that he should hold his peace: but he cried the more a great deal, Thou Son of David, have mercy on me. And Jesus stood still, and commanded him to be called. And they call the blind man, saying unto him, Be of good comfort, rise; he calleth thee.
Joh 10:3
To him the porter openeth; and the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out.
Php 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth: but he that hath mercy on the poor, happy is he.
corruption_summary: Bye, Felicia makes contemptuous dismissal a catchphrase; Scripture names contempt sin and shows a Lord who calls His sheep by name and stops for the dismissed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is contempt made fashionable. The meme trains users to treat people they find annoying as nameless extras in their story, to be waved off with a laugh. It flatters the speaker’s importance and shrinks the other person to a joke. That posture, multiplied across a culture, makes cruelty cool and kindness look weak. "He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth: but he that hath mercy on the poor, happy is he" (Pro 14:21).

The recovery is courtesy rooted in the image of God. A Christian can refuse a moocher’s request, leave a bad relationship, and end a conversation, all without contempt. Teach the young to set boundaries with words like "no, thank you," and to remember the names of people others ignore. The Lord who stopped for Bartimaeus while the crowd said "bye" is the model.
roots_summary: "God be with ye" → good-bye → bye + Latin felix (happy) → Felicia → Friday (1995) → c. 2014 meme.
roots_lines: Good-bye, contracted from "God be with ye" (16th c.)
Felicia, from Latin felix — happy, fortunate
1995: Friday, Ice Cube’s "Bye, Felicia"
c. 2014: viral meme; reality TV and social media
Biblical anchor: whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca (Mat 5:22); he calleth his own sheep by name (Joh 10:3)
usage: "He wanted to borrow money again? Bye, Felicia."
He that despiseth his neighbour sinneth (Pro 14:21).
The crowd said "bye" to Bartimaeus; Jesus stood still and called him (Mar 10:49).

etymology: From the military point (the lead soldier of a patrol, "on point," responsible for alertness and precision) and from the general sense of being exactly to the point. In 1990s hip-hop and AAVE, on point meant sharp, excellent, exactly right; the Millennial 2010s used it for anything well executed: a look, a joke, an essay, eyebrows ("brows on point"), often alongside on fleek (2014).
biblical_def: To be on point is to be exactly right, sharp, flawlessly executed: the outfit, the answer, the timing, the speech. It is a compliment to precision and excellence. The Christian observation: this is a good thing to admire, and Scripture admires it too. The right word at the right moment is a treasure: "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver" (Pro 25:11). The skilled craftsman is honoured: "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings" (Pro 22:29). The men of Issachar were "men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do" (1Ch 12:32), on point in their judgment. Daniel and his friends were "ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers" (Dan 1:20). God Himself does all things well: "He hath done all things well" (Mar 7:37). The only caution is about what we prize as on point. A culture can be precise about eyebrows and careless about character, sharp in its jokes and dull in its consciences. A father praises his children when they do something well, exactly and carefully; he teaches them excellence as a way of honouring God, "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord" (Col 3:23); and he helps them aim their precision at the things that matter most, so that their words, their work, and their lives are on point before Him.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (military and 1990s hip-hop origins) for exactly right, excellent, sharp; a redeemable admiration of precision that Scripture shares: a word fitly spoken (Pro 25:11), the diligent workman (Pro 22:29).
webster_full: ON POINT, adj. phr. (1990s hip-hop → Millennial slang, 2010s) Exactly right; excellent; well executed. "Your speech was on point." Related: on fleek.

Webster (1828), root point: POINT, noun [Latin punctum, from pungo, to prick, properly to thrust, preterit tense pepugi, showing that n is not radical.] 1. The sharp end of any instrument or body; as the point of a knife, of a sword or of a thorn. 2. A string with a tag; as a silken point 3. A small cape, headland or promontory; a tract of land extending into the sea, a lake or river, beyond the line of the shore, and becoming narrow at the end; as point Judith; Montauk point It is smaller than a cape. 4. The sting of an epigram; […]
Decode for parents: praise precision, and point it at character as well as appearance.
scriptures: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.

And of the children of Issachar, which were men that had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do; the heads of them were two hundred; and all their brethren were at their commandment.
Mar 7:37
And were beyond measure astonished, saying, He hath done all things well: he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
corruption_summary: On point admires excellence and precision; its only drift is precision about trifles while character is careless, which Scripture corrects by aiming excellence at God.
corruption_paragraphs: If there is a drift here, it is misplaced precision. The phrase is used most often of appearances: brows, outfits, makeup, photos. A culture that labours over the exact arch of an eyebrow may give little thought to whether its words are true or its promises kept. Excellence is good; but excellence spent only on surfaces is a misdirection of a gift.

The redemption is excellence for God’s glory. Bezaleel’s precise craftsmanship built the tabernacle; Daniel’s exact wisdom served a pagan king faithfully; Christ did all things well. Teach the young to do their work carefully and beautifully, to speak fitly, to understand the times, and to measure "on point" by the standard of the One who will one day say of faithful work, "Well done."
roots_summary: Latin punctum (a prick, a point) → point → military "on point" (lead of a patrol) → 1990s hip-hop on point (sharp, excellent) → 2010s Millennial praise.
roots_lines: Latin pungere — to prick; punctum — a point
Military: the soldier "on point" leads the patrol, alert and exact
1990s: hip-hop and AAVE on point — sharp, excellent
2010s: Millennial praise for anything well done; on fleek (2014)
Biblical anchor: a word fitly spoken (Pro 25:11); he hath done all things well (Mar 7:37)
usage: "Your timing on that joke was on point."
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver (Pro 25:11).
Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord (Col 3:23).

etymology: The ordinary adjective same used alone as a reply meaning "I feel exactly the same" or "that is me too." It became common on Tumblr and Twitter in the early 2010s as a response to relatable posts ("Same."), along with mood, big mood, relatable, and me. The one-word reply is a gesture of fellow-feeling: I recognize myself in what you said.
biblical_def: "Same" is the one-word reply that means "me too": you posted that you are tired, overwhelmed, craving pizza, or awkward at parties, and a friend writes, simply, "same." It is a small act of solidarity. The Christian observation: there is something precious in the impulse, and the gospel knows it well. Human beings are comforted to learn that they are not alone in their struggles. Paul writes, "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man" (1Co 10:13). The Church is meant to be a community where people can say "same" about their weaknesses and find company. "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). Above all, the Lord Jesus is the great "same" of the gospel: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin" (Heb 4:15). He became like us so that He could help us. There is also an ultimate Same in Scripture: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 13:8). The only caution is that "same" can stop at recognition and never move to help or change; shared complaint can become a club for staying stuck. A father welcomes his children’s honesty about struggle, says "same" when it is true, and then points them to the One who was tempted like us and can lift us.
webster_summary: Millennial one-word reply (early 2010s Tumblr and Twitter) meaning "I feel the same"; a small solidarity the gospel deepens: temptations common to man (1Co 10:13), a High Priest touched with our infirmities (Heb 4:15).
webster_full: SAME, interj. (Millennial social-media slang, early 2010s–present) A one-word reply meaning "I relate" or "that is true of me too." Related: mood, big mood, relatable, me.

Webster (1828), root same: SAME, adjective [Latin simul, together. Gr. Shall we suppose then that s has passed into an aspirate in this word, as in salt, Gr. or has the Greek word lost s? The word same may be the Latin idem or dem, dialectically varied. The primary sense is to set, to place, to put together.] 1. Identical; not different or other. Thou art the same and thy years shall have no end. Psalms 102:27 . The Lord Jesus, the same night in which he was betrayed, took bread. 1 Corinthians 11:23 . 2. […]
Decode for parents: "same" is fellow-feeling; help it move from shared complaint to shared help.
scriptures: There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
Heb 4:15
For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
Heb 13:8
Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
Gal 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
corruption_summary: Same is a small, good solidarity; its only drift is shared complaint that never moves to help or change, which Scripture answers with burden-bearing and a High Priest who helps.
corruption_paragraphs: The small drift in "same" is solidarity without movement. Online, relatability is currency, and posts that confess weakness collect "same" after "same" until weakness becomes an identity and a bonding ritual. A community of "same" can become a support group for staying the same. Real fellowship recognizes struggle and then helps: "Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2).

The redemption is that Christ’s "same" moves. He became the same as us in every way except sin so that He could rescue us, not merely sympathize. Teach the young to admit their weaknesses honestly, to tell friends "me too" when it helps them feel less alone, and then to say, "let’s pray about it," or "here’s what helped me." And teach them the Same who never changes: Jesus Christ, yesterday, today, and for ever.
roots_summary: Old Norse samr / Old English same (identical) → same → early-2010s one-word reply of relatability.
roots_lines: Old Norse samr — same; compare Greek homos
Early 2010s: Tumblr and Twitter reply "Same."
Related forms: mood, big mood, relatable, me
A gesture of fellow-feeling in a single word

Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever (Heb 13:8).

etymology: The past tense of shake used as an adjective for shaken: shocked, rattled, scared, or deeply surprised. The usage is old in AAVE and was spread by hip-hop, notably Mobb Deep’s "Shook Ones" (1995), where it meant scared or weak. In 2016–2017 it went mainstream on Twitter and in memes ("I’m shook") for anything surprising, from a plot twist to a celebrity breakup, and was added to online dictionaries.
biblical_def: To be shook is to be rattled: stunned by news, scared by something, or simply amazed. "That season finale had me shook." The Christian observation: the slang is harmless, and Scripture has a great deal to say about shaking. People are shaken by fear: when the disciples saw Jesus walking on the sea, "they were troubled, saying, It is a spirit; and they cried out for fear" (Mat 14:26). God Himself shakes things: at Philippi, "there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken" (Act 16:26). And He promises a final shaking of everything that can be shaken, "that those things which cannot be shaken may remain. Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace" (Heb 12:27-28). That is the deepest answer to being shook. The believer’s life can be rattled by bad news, but its foundation cannot be moved: "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved" (Psa 16:8). Some fear is right; the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, and it ought to shake us. But the fear of man and of circumstances is meant to give way to faith. A father tells his children: you will be shook by things in life, by losses, betrayals, and frightening news; when you are, run to the Rock that does not shake, and you will find that the kingdom you belong to cannot be moved.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (AAVE; Mobb Deep, 1995; mainstream 2016–2017) for shocked or rattled; harmless, and an opening to Scripture’s kingdom which cannot be moved (Heb 12:28; Psa 16:8).
webster_full: SHOOK, adj. (AAVE; Millennial and Gen Z slang, mainstream 2016–present; past tense of shake used for shaken) Shocked, rattled, scared, or amazed. "I’m shook."

Webster (1828), root shake: SHAKE, verb transitive preterit tense shook ; participle passive shaken . 1. To cause to move with quick vibrations; to move rapidly one way and the other; to agitate; as, the wind shakes a tree; an earthquake shakes the hills or the earth. I shook my lap, and said, so God shake out every man from his house- Nehemiah 5:13 He shook the sacred honors of his head. Dryden . -As a fig casteth her untimely fruit, when it is shaken of a mighty wind. Revelation 6:1 . 2. To make to totter or tremble. […]
Decode for parents: harmless; when your child is truly shaken, point to the Rock that does not move.
scriptures: And when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, It is a spirit; and they cried out for fear.
And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's bands were loosed.

And this word, Yet once more, signifieth the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain. Wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear:
Psa 16:8
I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.
Psa 62:2
He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved.
corruption_summary: Shook is harmless slang for being rattled; Scripture turns it to the deeper truth that believers belong to a kingdom which cannot be shaken.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct in the word. The only drift worth noting is the habit of being perpetually shook: a culture of constant news, outrage, and spectacle keeps young people rattled, startled from one shock to the next, with little sense of anything stable beneath them. Anxiety becomes a lifestyle.

The redemption is a foundation. "He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved" (Psa 62:2). Teach the young to take shocks seriously without being ruled by them, to bring their fears to God, and to build their lives on what cannot be shaken: the Word, the promises, the kingdom of Christ. Then they can be shook for a moment without being moved.
roots_summary: Old English scacan (to shake), past scoc → shook → AAVE adjectival shook (shaken) → 1995 "Shook Ones" → 2016–2017 mainstream.
roots_lines: Old English scacan, past tense scoc — shook
AAVE: shook as adjective — scared, shaken
1995: Mobb Deep, "Shook Ones"
2016–2017: Twitter "I’m shook"; online dictionaries
Biblical anchor: a kingdom which cannot be moved (Heb 12:28); I shall not be moved (Psa 16:8)
usage: "That ending had me shook."
I have set the LORD always before me; I shall not be moved (Psa 16:8).
We receive a kingdom which cannot be moved (Heb 12:28).

etymology: Clipped from family. In AAVE and hip-hop from the 1990s, fam meant close friends regarded as family; it also became central to London Multicultural English ("you get me, fam?"). In the 2010s it spread across Millennial and Gen Z speech as a term of address and affection for friends ("thanks, fam"), and the phrase "squad and fam" covered one’s inner circle.
biblical_def: Fam is family, extended to friends: the people close enough to be called kin. "Love you, fam." "What’s good, fam?" The Christian observation: the word reaches for something deeply biblical, and the gospel fulfils it. God builds families, "God setteth the solitary in families" (Psa 68:6), and the Church is a household where strangers become kin. "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God" (Eph 2:19). The Lord Jesus redefined family around Himself: "For whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and mother" (Mar 3:35). Believers are adopted children of one Father and call each other brother and sister, which is exactly what "fam" means. Paul tells Timothy to treat "the elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity" (1Ti 5:2). The slang also shows a longing. Many young people use "fam" for friends because their own families are broken or absent, and the friends have had to stand in. That is a sorrow the Church should see and answer. A father loves his own family first, as Scripture commands, and also teaches his children to open their home and church to friends who need a fam, so that the word becomes true: brothers and sisters in Christ, sharing tables and burdens.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (1990s AAVE and hip-hop; 2010s mainstream) clipped from family, for close friends as kin; redeemable, for the Church is the household of God (Eph 2:19) where those who do His will are brother and sister (Mar 3:35).
webster_full: FAM, n. (AAVE and hip-hop, 1990s; Millennial and Gen Z slang, 2010s–present; clipped from family) Close friends regarded as family; used in address. "Thanks, fam."

Webster (1828), root family: FAMILY, noun [Latin familia.] 1. The collective body of persons who live in one house and under one head or manager; a household, including parents, children and servants, and as the case may be, lodgers or boarders. 2. Those who descend from one common progenitor; a tribe or race; kindred; lineage. Thus the Israelites were a branch of the family of Abraham; and the descendants of Reuben, of Manasseh, etc., were called their families. The whole human race are the family of Adam, the human family 3. Course of descent; […]
Decode for parents: when a friend calls your child "fam," ask whether that friend has a family; your table may be the answer.
scriptures: Psa 68:6
God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land.
Eph 2:19
Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God;
Mar 3:35
For whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and mother.
The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.
Gal 6:10
As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
corruption_summary: Fam reaches for kinship among friends, often because families are broken; the gospel fulfils it in the household of God and calls Christian homes to take in the solitary.
corruption_paragraphs: If there is a corruption here, it is not in the word but in what it often replaces. Many young people call friends "fam" because their homes have failed them: absent fathers, divorce, distance. Friends become family by necessity. Sometimes the "fam" is a gang or a crew with its own loyalties and dangers. The longing is good; the substitutes can be fragile or worse.

The redemption is the Church as a real family and Christian homes as open doors. "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith" (Gal 6:10). Teach the young to honour their own families, to be faithful friends, and to bring their friends into the household of God, where the word "fam" is literally true: one Father, one Lord, brothers and sisters for ever.
roots_summary: Latin familia (household) → family → 1990s AAVE / hip-hop fam → London MLE → 2010s Millennial and Gen Z address.
roots_lines: Latin familia — a household, servants and kin
1990s: AAVE and hip-hop fam — close friends as family
2000s: London Multicultural English "you get me, fam?"
2010s: general Millennial and Gen Z term of address
Biblical anchor: the household of God (Eph 2:19); whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother (Mar 3:35)
usage: "Appreciate you, fam."
Ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but of the household of God (Eph 2:19).
God setteth the solitary in families (Psa 68:6): open your table.

etymology: A dialect form of swollen (via swoll), used in AAVE and bodybuilding slang from the 1990s for very muscular, pumped up. It spread in 2000s–2010s gym culture and internet humour ("Do you even lift, bro?", "get swole"), and with the "swole doge" meme of the 2020s. Related: jacked, ripped, yoked, gains.
biblical_def: To be swole is to be big, muscular, pumped: the product of heavy lifting and many protein shakes. "He got swole over the summer." The Christian observation: strength is a good gift, and training the body is not a sin. Scripture admires strong men: David’s mighty men, Samson’s God-given strength, the craftsman’s arms. Paul uses athletic discipline as an image of the Christian life: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection" (1Co 9:27). And he grants that "bodily exercise profiteth little" (1Ti 4:8): little, but not nothing. A young man who lifts to be strong for work, protection, and service is stewarding his body. The examination concerns the heart. Gym culture easily becomes a religion of the body, with its own liturgy, diet laws, and confessions, and its own idol: the mirror. Scripture deflates that worship: the LORD "delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man. The LORD taketh pleasure in them that fear him" (Psa 147:10-11). Samson, the swolest man in the Bible, was undone by his appetites, and his strength was a gift on loan. A father lifts with his son and teaches him to be strong, disciplined, and humble: strong to carry the weak, disciplined in body as an image of discipline in soul, and humble enough to know that the strength comes from God and that godliness profits far more.
webster_summary: Millennial gym slang (1990s AAVE and bodybuilding, from swollen) for very muscular; strength and training are good stewardship (1Co 9:27), but the LORD delighteth not in the legs of a man, and the body can become an idol (Psa 147:10-11).
webster_full: SWOLE, adj. (AAVE and bodybuilding slang, 1990s; Millennial gym culture, 2000s–2010s; from swollen) Very muscular; pumped up from training. "Get swole." Related: jacked, ripped, gains.
No Webster 1828 entry located for the root swell in the online edition.
Decode for parents: encourage strength and discipline; watch for the mirror becoming an altar.
scriptures: But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man. The LORD taketh pleasure in them that fear him, in those that hope in his mercy.

That he told her all his heart, and said unto her, There hath not come a razor upon mine head; for I have been a Nazarite unto God from my mother's womb: if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me, and I shall become weak, and be like any other man.
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
corruption_summary: Swole celebrates strength, a good gift; gym culture can make the body an idol and the mirror an altar, which Scripture deflates: the LORD takes pleasure in them that fear Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is body-worship. Lifting can become an identity, a moral system, and a source of pride, with hours in the mirror and a hierarchy of men by size. It can also slide into dangerous shortcuts, steroids and extreme diets, and into contempt for weaker men. Samson’s story is the warning: "if I be shaven, then my strength will go from me" (Jdg 16:17). He thought the strength was his; it was always the Lord’s.

The recovery is strength as service. A strong body is a tool for work, protection, and helping others, and training it is a lesson in discipline that serves the soul. Teach young men to lift for strength and health, to stay humble, and to wait on the One who renews strength: "they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles" (Isa 40:31).
roots_summary: Old English swellan (to swell) → swollen → dialect swoll → 1990s AAVE and bodybuilding swole → 2000s–2010s gym and internet slang.

Dialect swoll, swole — swollen
1990s: AAVE and bodybuilding swole — very muscular
2000s–2010s: gym memes, "Do you even lift?"; 2020s "swole doge"
Biblical anchor: I keep under my body (1Co 9:27); he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man (Psa 147:10)
usage: "He’s been lifting every day; he’s getting swole."
Bodily exercise profiteth little; godliness is profitable unto all things (1Ti 4:8).
The LORD taketh pleasure in them that fear him (Psa 147:11).

etymology: From gain (to obtain, to increase). In bodybuilding and weightlifting forums of the 2000s and gym culture of the 2010s, gains meant measurable increases in muscle size or strength ("making gains," "sick gains," "#gains"). It spread to any improvement ("gains in my savings") and to meme culture ("Do you even lift, bro?"). Related: swole, bulking, cutting, PR (personal record).
biblical_def: Gains are progress in the gym: added muscle, added weight on the bar, a new personal record. The word can stretch to any measurable improvement. The Christian observation: progress through discipline is good, and Scripture often uses the language of gain. But it asks a question that puts all our gains in perspective: "For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" (Mar 8:36). Paul, who had a résumé of religious gains, wrote, "But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord" (Php 3:7-8). And he named the greatest gain: "But godliness with contentment is great gain" (1Ti 6:6). That does not make physical progress worthless. A young man who disciplines himself to train, eat well, and keep at it is learning patience and perseverance that will serve him in harder things. Scripture itself uses the athlete as a picture of faithfulness: "every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things" (1Co 9:25). The danger is the scoreboard that never stops: gains as the measure of a man, the next PR as the meaning of the week. A father celebrates his son’s gains, lifts beside him, and asks him now and then about the other gains: in prayer, in patience, in kindness, in knowing Christ, the ones that last.
webster_summary: Millennial gym slang (2000s forums; 2010s) for increases in muscle or strength; disciplined progress is good (1Co 9:25), but Scripture weighs every gain against the soul (Mar 8:36) and names godliness with contentment the great gain (1Ti 6:6).
webster_full: GAINS, n. pl. (Millennial gym slang, 2000s–present) Increases in muscle mass or strength from training; by extension, any measurable progress. "Making gains." "#gains."

Webster (1828), root gain: GAIN, noun Profit; interest; something obtained as an advantage. But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. Philippians 3:7 . 1. Unlawful advantage. 2 Corinthians 12:17 . 2. Overplus in computation; any thing opposed to loss.
Decode for parents: celebrate the gym gains; ask about the soul’s gains too.
scriptures: Mar 8:36
For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?

But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
But godliness with contentment is great gain.
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
corruption_summary: Gains rightly prizes disciplined progress, but can make the scoreboard the measure of a man; Scripture counts all gain loss for Christ and calls godliness with contentment great gain.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the endless scoreboard. Gym culture, especially online, measures worth in numbers: lifts, sizes, body-fat percentages, followers for the physique. The chase is never finished, and it can consume hours, money, and attention that belong elsewhere. Paul’s list of former gains reminds us that even good achievements can become things we trust in place of Christ.

The recovery is ordered progress. "For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come" (1Ti 4:8). Train the body; train the soul more. Teach young men to set goals, work patiently, and enjoy their progress, while keeping the larger ledger in view, where the only gain that counts for eternity is the knowledge of Christ.
roots_summary: Old French gaaignier (to earn, to cultivate) → gain (profit, increase) → 2000s bodybuilding forums gains → 2010s gym slang and memes.

Middle English gain — profit, advantage

usage: "Six months of squats and the gains are real."
What shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? (Mar 8:36).
Godliness with contentment is great gain (1Ti 6:6).

etymology: A list of things to do before one dies, from kick the bucket (to die, recorded from the eighteenth century, of uncertain origin). The phrase existed in the 2000s but was popularized by the 2007 film The Bucket List (Jack Nicholson and Morgan Freeman as two terminally ill men pursuing a list of adventures). Millennials made the bucket list a staple of travel and self-development culture: skydiving, the Northern Lights, Machu Picchu, a marathon.
biblical_def: A bucket list is a list of experiences to have before you die: places to see, thrills to try, goals to achieve. It treats life as a set of boxes to tick before the end. The Christian observation: the bucket list takes death seriously, which is more than much of the culture does, and Scripture commends that seriousness. "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Psa 90:12). There is nothing wrong with wanting to see the Grand Canyon or to run a marathon; God made a world full of wonders. But the bucket list often rests on a quiet assumption: that this life is all there is, so experiences must be crammed in before the lights go out. Scripture tells of a man with a bucket list of a kind: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Luk 12:19-20). The Preacher tried everything on his list and concluded, "all was vanity and vexation of spirit" (Ecc 2:11). The Christian has a different kind of list, because death is not the end: Paul’s was, "to live is Christ, and to die is gain" (Php 1:21). A father helps his children dream of wonderful things to see and do, and teaches them that the best item on any list is to know Christ, and that for those in Him, the world to come will make the most spectacular bucket list look small.
webster_summary: Millennial-era phrase (from kick the bucket; popularized by the 2007 film) for experiences to have before dying; it rightly numbers our days (Psa 90:12), but often assumes this life is all, against Christ, for whom to die is gain (Php 1:21).
webster_full: BUCKET LIST, n. (popularized 2007; Millennial travel and self-development culture) A list of experiences or achievements a person hopes to accomplish before dying. From kick the bucket.

Webster (1828), root bucket: BUCKET, noun 1. The vessel in which water is drawn out of a well; it is nearly in the form of a pail. 2. A vessel or pail used at sea to draw water up at the side of a ship, for washing the decks, etc. 3. A vessel made of leather, nearly in the form of a pail, but narrower and deeper, used to convey water by hand for extinguishing fires.
Decode for parents: let your children dream; make sure Christ is first on the list and eternity is in the frame.
scriptures: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.

And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
Ecc 2:11
Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.
Php 1:21
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.
corruption_summary: The bucket list takes death seriously but often assumes this life is all, cramming experience before the end; Scripture numbers our days for wisdom and promises a world to come.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is experience as salvation. When there is nothing after death, life becomes a race to collect sensations before time runs out, and a bucket list is its scorecard. Missing an item feels like a loss that can never be made up. The rich fool of Jesus’ parable had the same horizon, and God called him a fool not for enjoying good things but for living as if his soul would not be required of him.

The recovery is eternity in view. "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him" (1Co 2:9). Christians can enjoy the wonders of this world without panic, because they are previews, not the main event. Teach the young to make lists of good things to do, especially things to do for others, and to hold the list loosely, knowing that the best is yet to come.
roots_summary: Old English buc (pitcher) / Old French buket → bucket → 18th-c. idiom kick the bucket (die) → 2007 film The Bucket List → Millennial travel culture.

usage: "Seeing the Northern Lights is on my bucket list."
Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee (Luk 12:20).
Eye hath not seen … the things which God hath prepared (1Co 2:9).

etymology: A German compound, wandern (to hike, to roam) + Lust (desire, joy), borrowed into English in the early twentieth century for a strong desire to travel. It had a quiet life until the 2010s, when it became a defining Instagram hashtag and tattoo of Millennial travel culture: backpacking, solo trips, "wanderlust" captions under sunsets in Bali and Iceland, and a whole lifestyle of experiences over possessions.
biblical_def: Wanderlust is the itch to travel: to see new places, to be on the road, to collect countries and sunsets. For Millennials it became an identity and an aesthetic, the backpack, the passport stamps, the caption under the cliff-edge photo. The Christian observation: the desire to see God’s world is good. "The earth is the LORD’s, and the fulness thereof" (Psa 24:1), and travel can open the eyes to His creativity and to the breadth of His people. Abraham went out "not knowing whither he went" (Heb 11:8), and the apostles crossed the known world. But Scripture distinguishes the pilgrim from the wanderer. The pilgrim travels toward a destination: the patriarchs "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth … they seek a country" (Heb 11:13-14). The wanderer simply moves. Scripture is not romantic about restless wandering. Cain was sentenced to be "a fugitive and a vagabond" (Gen 4:12); "As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place" (Pro 27:8); and God said of a faithless people, "Thus have they loved to wander, they have not refrained their feet" (Jer 14:10). Wanderlust can be a symptom of a heart that has not found rest and hopes the next place will supply it. A father can take his children to see the world and teach them that the deepest longing behind wanderlust is a longing for home, the city with foundations whose builder and maker is God.
webster_summary: German loan (early 20th c.) turned Millennial travel identity (2010s Instagram) for the strong desire to roam; seeing God’s world is good (Psa 24:1), but Scripture distinguishes the pilgrim seeking a country (Heb 11:13-14) from the restless wanderer (Pro 27:8).
webster_full: WANDERLUST, n. (German loan, early 20th c.; Millennial travel culture, 2010s) A strong desire to travel and explore. Popular as a hashtag, caption, and tattoo; related travel bug, digital nomad.

Webster (1828), root wander: WANDER, verb intransitive [G., to wander to walk, to change, exchange or transform.] 1. To rove; to ramble here and there without any certain course or object in view; as, to wander over the fields; to wander about the town, or about the country. Men may sometimes wander for amusement or exercise. Persons sometimes wander because they have no home and are wretched, and sometimes because they have no occupation. They wandered about in sheep-skins and goat-skins. Hebrews 11:37 . He wandereth abroad for bread. Job 15:23 . […]
Decode for parents: travel well with your children, and teach them the difference between a pilgrim and a wanderer.
scriptures: Psa 24:1
The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country.
Pro 27:8
As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place.

Thus saith the LORD unto this people, Thus have they loved to wander, they have not refrained their feet, therefore the LORD doth not accept them; he will now remember their iniquity, and visit their sins.
For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
corruption_summary: Wanderlust can be healthy delight in God’s world or a restless heart hoping the next place will bring rest; Scripture blesses the pilgrim and warns the wanderer.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is restlessness baptized as adventure. The Millennial travel aesthetic often sold movement as meaning: if life feels empty, go somewhere new. But the soul travels with the traveller. Augustine’s line is the diagnosis: our hearts are restless till they rest in God. A life of constant movement can also avoid the commitments that make a life: a church, a marriage, a neighbourhood, a vocation rooted in one place.

The redemption is pilgrimage. Abraham travelled because he "looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God" (Heb 11:10). Christians can travel gladly, to see wonders, serve missions, and visit the Church around the world, while staying rooted in a local body and a home. Teach the young that the road is good when it leads somewhere, and that the true home they long for is not a place on the map but the presence of God.
roots_summary: German wandern (to roam) + Lust (desire) → Wanderlust → English (early 20th c.) → 2010s Instagram travel identity.
roots_lines: Old English wandrian / German wandern — to roam
German Lust — desire, pleasure
Early 20th c.: borrowed into English
2010s: Instagram hashtag, tattoo, travel lifestyle
Biblical anchor: strangers and pilgrims … they seek a country (Heb 11:13-14); a man that wandereth from his place (Pro 27:8)
usage: "Her bio just says ‘wanderlust’ and has a plane emoji."
As a bird that wandereth from her nest, so is a man that wandereth from his place (Pro 27:8).
They seek a country (Heb 11:14): pilgrims, not wanderers.

etymology: A remote worker who uses the internet to work from anywhere while travelling. The term was popularized by the 1997 book Digital Nomad by Tsugio Makimoto and David Manners, which predicted that technology would free workers from fixed locations. In the 2010s it became a Millennial lifestyle and industry: laptops on beaches in Bali, co-working spaces in Chiang Mai and Lisbon, travel blogs, and visas designed for remote workers. The 2020 shift to remote work multiplied its numbers.
biblical_def: A digital nomad works from a laptop while moving from city to city or country to country: answering email in Bali, coding in Lisbon, posting sunsets from Mexico. It is the Millennial dream of freedom from the office and the suburb. The Christian observation: remote work itself is neutral, and travel can be a gift. Paul worked as a tentmaker while moving between cities, and his travels served the gospel. But the nomadic life raises questions Scripture cares about. The first is rootedness. Even the patriarchs, who lived in tents, travelled as households with altars, and when God sent His people into a foreign land He told them to put down roots: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens … And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away" (Jer 29:5, 7). The second is community. A Christian cannot follow Christ alone. "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together" (Heb 10:25) assumes a church one actually belongs to, with elders who know your name and brothers who know your sins. A digital nomad passing through a dozen cities a year can easily belong to none. The third is marriage and children, which need a place. A father can admire the adventure and still tell his son: freedom is not the absence of attachments; it is the right ones. Work hard wherever you are, but be someone’s neighbour, some church’s member, and, God willing, some child’s father in a home they can call their own.
webster_summary: Millennial lifestyle term (1997 book; 2010s boom; 2020 surge) for remote workers who travel continually; remote work is neutral, but Scripture calls believers to rooted community, church membership, and seeking the peace of a place (Jer 29:5-7; Heb 10:25).
webster_full: DIGITAL NOMAD, n. (term popularized 1997; Millennial lifestyle, 2010s–present) A person who works remotely via the internet while travelling from place to place. Related: remote work, co-working, wanderlust.

Webster (1828), root nomad: NOMAD, noun [Gr. Living on pasturage, to distribute or divide, to feed. This verb is connected with Latin Nemus, a wood, a place over-grown with trees, and also a pasture, the primary sense of which is probably to spring or shoot, for the verb signifies among other things, to leap, to dance, and may be allied to Eng. nimble. Cattle originally subsisted by browsing, as they still do in new settlements.] One who leads a wandering life, and subsists by tending herds of cattle which graze on herbage of spontaneous growth. […]
Decode for parents: affirm the skills; ask where your child belongs to a church and who knows him by name.
scriptures: Act 18:3
And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
Jer 29:5
Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them;
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
Psa 68:6
God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land.
corruption_summary: Digital nomadism prizes freedom from place and attachment; Scripture honours work and travel but calls believers to roots, a church that knows them, and households that need a home.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is freedom defined as unattachment. The digital nomad ideal sells a life with no fixed obligations: no office, no lease, no local community, no one depending on you. It is attractive to the young and often lonely in practice. It can postpone marriage and children indefinitely, and it makes church membership nearly impossible. A life without roots is a life without the soil in which much Christian virtue grows.

The recovery is mission and membership. Paul travelled for the gospel and stayed for years in places like Corinth and Ephesus, building churches; he was never a tourist. "And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers" (Act 18:3). Christians may work remotely and travel, and they should do it as people who belong somewhere: to a local church, to a family, to a place whose peace they seek. Teach the young that roots are not a cage but a gift.
roots_summary: Greek nomas (roaming in search of pasture) → nomad + Latin digitus (finger) → digital → 1997 book Digital Nomad → 2010s Millennial lifestyle → 2020 remote-work surge.

Latin digitus — finger, numeral → digital

usage: "She’s a digital nomad; last month Lisbon, this month Mexico City."
Seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried (Jer 29:7).
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together (Heb 10:25).
